t: Number of Ways to Paint N × 3 Grid — Row-Type DP
o:
Each row is a length-3 sequence of colors where horizontally adjacent cells differ. There are only **12** valid row patterns: 6 of type ABA (first and third color equal) and 6 of type ABC (all three distinct). A new row can follow a previous row iff they differ column-by-column. So instead of tracking all $3^3 = 27$ raw rows, we track counts per *pattern type*.

For n = 1 the answer is simply 12 (6 ABA + 6 ABC). For n = 5000, brute-forcing $12^{4999}$ grids is impossible, but a DP over just two aggregate counts runs in linear time — this is why the constraints hint at an aggregated DP rather than enumeration.
k: Every valid row is either pattern ABA (colors[0]==colors[2], 6 ways) or ABC (all distinct, 6 ways).
Transitions depend only on the previous row's type, not its exact colors: from ABA there are 3 ABA + 2 ABC continuations; from ABC there are 2 ABA + 2 ABC continuations.
The answer for n rows satisfies f(n) = 5·f(n-1) - 2·f(n-2), giving an O(log n) closed-form via fast exponentiation if needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all valid grids
a.i: Enumerate every coloring cell by cell: pick a color for each cell that differs from its left and top neighbors, recursing through the grid. This directly models the problem and works for tiny n, but the search space grows like $3^{3n}$ in the worst case (pruned by adjacency), so it is far too slow for n up to 5000. It serves as a correctness baseline.
s: Recursively fill cells in row-major order.
At each cell try each of the 3 colors, skipping any equal to the left or top neighbor.
When the grid is full, count it as one way.
a.t: Exponential in practice (~O(3^(3n)) nodes before pruning) — only feasible for very small n.
a.sp: O(n) recursion depth plus the O(3n) grid.

a.n: Approach 2: Aggregated DP over row types (optimal)
a.i: Classify each valid row as ABA (ends match, 6 instances) or ABC (all distinct, 6 instances). By symmetry, the number of valid continuations depends only on the previous row's *type*: after an ABA row there are 3 same-type continuations and 2 opposite-type ones; after an ABC row there are 2 of each. Track counts (a, b) = (#ABA-ending, #ABC-ending prefixes) and update row by row. Start with (6, 6); answer is a + b mod 1e9+7.
s: Initialize a = b = 6 (one-row prefixes ending in each type).
For each of the remaining n-1 rows set a' = 3a + 2b, b' = 2a + 2b, taking mod 1e9+7.
After processing all rows return (a + b) mod 1e9+7.
(Optional) note the recurrence f(n) = 5f(n-1) - 2f(n-2), enabling O(log n) matrix power if n were huge.
a.t: O(n) time — one constant-time transition per row.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force idea briefly to show you understand the structure, then pivot immediately to the aggregated DP — it is the expected solution and trivially handles n = 5000. Common pitfalls: forgetting that both row types have exactly 6 colorings (not 3), miscounting transitions (verify by hand on one ABA row: e.g., 121 extends to 131, 212, 232, 313, 323 → three ABA, two ABC), and missing the modulo on intermediate sums. Edge cases: n = 1 must return 12. Follow-ups: derive the O(log n) matrix-exponentiation solution using f(n) = 5f(n-1) − 2f(n-2), generalize to m columns or k colors, or count grids where specific cells are pre-colored.
